articles.title: The Rise of Quantum Computing
articles.description: Quantum computing is set to revolutionize how researchers solve complex optimization and simulation problems.
articles.body:
For seventy years, computing progress has meant one thing: making classical bits smaller, faster and cheaper. Quantum computing doesn't continue that story — it starts a different one. Instead of shrinking the switch, it changes what the switch is. The result is a machine that's useless for most of what your laptop does, and potentially transformative for a narrow set of problems classical hardware will never finish computing.

This is a practical tour of where quantum computing actually stands in 2026: the physics in plain language, the engineering wall the field is climbing, the problems that genuinely benefit, the ones that don't, and what a technology team should do about it today.

What a qubit really is

A classical bit gives you a definite answer: 0 or 1. A qubit is a description of how likely each answer becomes when you finally look. Before measurement, the qubit holds a combination — a superposition — of both states, weighted by numbers called amplitudes. Amplitudes can be negative or complex, and that's the whole trick.

Because amplitudes can be negative, wrong answers can cancel each other out. A quantum algorithm is essentially a carefully choreographed interference pattern: you arrange the computation so the paths leading to incorrect results destructively interfere, and the paths leading to the correct one reinforce each other. Then you measure, and the right answer is overwhelmingly likely to fall out.

Two more properties matter here:

  • Entanglement. Qubits can be correlated so the state of the group can't be described by listing each qubit separately. This is what makes the state space grow exponentially — 300 entangled qubits describe more amplitudes than there are atoms in the observable universe.
  • Measurement collapse. You never get to read the amplitudes directly. You get one sample. Everything clever about quantum algorithm design is really about squeezing useful information out of a single classical readout.

That last constraint is the reason quantum computers aren't "parallel computers that try every answer at once." They explore every path, sure, but you only get to keep one — so the algorithm has to make sure the one you keep is worth having.

The hardware race: four bets, no winner yet

Nobody has settled on how to physically build a qubit. Four approaches dominate serious investment right now, and each one trades away something different to get there.

Superconducting circuits

The approach behind most headline machines. Tiny loops of superconducting metal, cooled to roughly 15 millikelvin — colder than deep space — behave as artificial atoms with controllable energy levels. Gates are fast (tens of nanoseconds) and the fabrication borrows heavily from the semiconductor industry. The cost is fragility: coherence times measured in hundreds of microseconds, and a dilution refrigerator the size of a small car.

Trapped ions

Individual charged atoms suspended in electromagnetic fields and manipulated with lasers. Every qubit is identical because nature manufactured it, coherence lasts seconds rather than microseconds, and any ion can interact with any other. The trade-off is speed: gates run thousands of times slower than superconducting ones, and scaling past a few dozen ions per trap means shuttling atoms between zones.

Photonics

Qubits encoded in light, operating at or near room temperature and naturally suited to networking between machines. The difficulty is that photons barely interact with each other, so two-qubit gates rely on measurement-based tricks that are probabilistic and hungry for extra resources.

Neutral atoms

The fastest-moving newcomer. Arrays of atoms held in optical tweezers can be rearranged into arbitrary geometries and scaled into the thousands, with excitation into high-energy Rydberg states providing the interaction. Control precision is improving quickly, and the flexible connectivity turns out to be unusually well suited to error-correcting codes.

Error correction is the entire game

If there's one thing to understand about this field's timeline, it's this: raw qubit counts are marketing, and logical qubit counts are engineering.

Physical qubits fail constantly. Typical two-qubit gate error rates sit near one in a thousand — a rate that would make a classical CPU completely unusable. Useful algorithms need error rates around one in a trillion. That gap of nine orders of magnitude gets closed by quantum error correction: spreading one logical qubit across many physical qubits, then continuously measuring the relationships between them to detect errors without measuring — and therefore destroying — the encoded data itself.

Quantum error correction works by asking the system questions it can answer without revealing its secret: not "what state are you in?" but "did neighbours three and four just disagree?"

The dominant scheme, the surface code, needs somewhere between hundreds and a few thousand physical qubits per logical qubit, depending on hardware quality. A cryptographically relevant machine therefore implies millions of physical qubits. The genuinely good news is that this is no longer theoretical: experiments have crossed the threshold where adding more physical qubits to a logical patch makes it better rather than worse. The scaling law now points the right direction. The remaining work is enormous, but it's engineering now, not physics.

What it's actually good for

Quantum computing is a specialist instrument, not a general-purpose upgrade. Here's the honest shortlist:

Simulating quantum systems

The original motivation, and still the strongest case by a wide margin. Molecules, catalysts and superconductors are quantum systems, and classical computers can only approximate them at exponential cost. Nitrogen fixation, battery electrochemistry and drug binding affinity are all bottlenecked by the accuracy of these simulations. A fault-tolerant machine of even modest logical size would be genuinely transformative here — arguably worth the entire investment on its own.

Cryptography — in both directions

Shor's algorithm factors large integers efficiently, which breaks RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography outright. No machine remotely capable of running it exists yet, but the "harvest now, decrypt later" threat is real: data intercepted today can just sit in storage until a capable machine eventually shows up. That's exactly why post-quantum cryptography standards are already finalised, and why migration is a present-tense infrastructure task, not a someday problem.

Optimisation and machine learning — with caveats

The most oversold category, by far. Quantum approaches to logistics, portfolio construction and training acceleration are heavily researched, but classical algorithms and hardware keep improving too, and several claimed quantum advantages have already been erased by better classical methods. Treat vendor claims in this space with a lot more scepticism than you'd apply to the chemistry claims.

What a technology team should actually do in 2026

  1. Inventory your cryptography. Know exactly where RSA and ECC live in your stack — TLS termination, code signing, VPNs, stored archives, embedded devices. It's unglamorous work, and it's the single highest-value quantum-related task available today.
  2. Plan post-quantum migration by data lifetime. Anything that has to stay confidential beyond a decade should move to standardised post-quantum algorithms now, typically in hybrid mode alongside the classical ones.
  3. Learn the problem shapes, not the hardware. The durable skill is recognising which of your problems have the structure quantum methods actually exploit. Hardware will keep churning; that judgement won't.
  4. Prototype on simulators. Open toolkits let engineers write and test circuits without touching real hardware at all. Thirty simulated qubits on a laptop is plenty to build real intuition.
  5. Ignore qubit-count press releases. Ask instead about gate fidelity, coherence time, connectivity and logical qubit demonstrations. Those four numbers predict progress. The headline number doesn't.

The realistic timeline

Near term, expect steady growth in logical qubit demonstrations and increasingly credible chemistry results on small molecules, alongside continued incremental hardware records. The middle of the horizon should bring early fault-tolerant machines capable of scientifically meaningful simulation that classical hardware simply can't match. Cryptographically relevant machines remain further out still, and depend on error-correction overhead falling faster than currently projected.

The useful mental model here isn't "quantum replaces classical." It's the GPU: a specialised accelerator that sits beside conventional infrastructure, gets invoked through an API for the narrow slice of work where it dominates, and stays irrelevant for everything else. Most developers will never write a quantum circuit themselves — they'll call a service that used one to design a better catalyst, a better battery, or a better drug.

That's a smaller claim than the hype suggests, and a far more interesting one than the scepticism allows.
